title: Tensor learning with orthogonal, Lorentz, and symplectic symmetries
claim: Equivariant outputs can be built as a learned weighted sum of tensor products of the inputs plus isotropic tensors.
layout: Left-to-right flow, 3 stages; inputs, tensor products, summed output, with an isotropic tensor branch
description: The figure shows how an equivariant tensor function is built from four input vectors. On the left, v1 to v4 are stacked colored columns. A bold arrow leads to a 4x4 grid of colored cells labeled 'Dot products of inputs'. On the right, under the heading 'Tensor products of inputs', is a row of terms: a coefficient q_{0,(),(1,1)} multiplied by a small colored matrix, then the 3x3 tensor product v1⊗v1, then plus signs and the same pattern for v1⊗v2 and v1⊗v3, ending in an ellipsis. Thin lines run from these terms down to a large sigma labeled 'output', next to a 3x3 colored output matrix. A final branch labeled 'Isotropic tensors' has coefficient q_{1,(),()} and a gray identity-like matrix labeled id. Pastel colors tie the cells to one another. The eye goes first to the colorful grids.
caption: Illustration of the method from Corollary [ref] with 4 input vectors in $\mathbb R^3$ and a \tensor{2}{+} output. The tensor product of inputs includes all 16 possible tensor products of ordered pairs of input vectors, plus the isotropic Kronecker delta, labeled $id$. The coefficients $q_{t,\sigma,J}$ shown here use $\sigma=()$, the identity permutation in $S_{k'}$.
abstract: Tensors are a fundamental data structure for many scientific contexts, such as time series analysis, materials science, and physics, among many others. Improving our ability to produce and handle tensors is essential to efficiently address problems in these domains. In this paper, we show how to exploit the underlying symmetries of functions that map tensors to tensors. More concretely, we develop universally expressive equivariant machine learning architectures on tensors that exploit that, in many cases, these tensor functions are equivariant with respect to the diagonal action of the orthogonal, Lorentz, and/or symplectic groups. We showcase our results on three problems coming from material science, theoretical computer science, and time series analysis. For time series, we combine our method with the increasingly popular path signatures approach, which is also invariant with respect to reparameterizations. Our numerical experiments show that our equivariant models perform better than corresponding non-equivariant baselines.
